title: Standard Deviation of a Random Variable
short: Measure how much a random variable typically varies from its mean.

blocks.html: Two games can have the same expected value and feel completely different: one pays about the same every time, the other swings wildly. The standard deviation you learned for data has a twin for random variables.

The variance of a discrete random variable is $$\sigma^2 = \sum (x - \mu)^2 P(x),$$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$, a typical distance of $X$ from its mean. A shortcut: $\sigma^2 = E(X^2) - \mu^2$.

It is the data formula with probabilities in place of "divide by the count": each squared distance from the mean is weighted by how often it happens in the long run. (No $n - 1$ appears, because here we know the true probabilities and the true mean.) The shortcut comes from expanding $(x - \mu)^2 = x^2 - 2\mu x + \mu^2$ and using $\sum xP(x) = \mu$ and $\sum P(x) = 1$.

blocks.title: A small distribution
blocks.q: $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities $0.25, 0.5, 0.25$. Find $\sigma$.

blocks.title: One die
blocks.q: Find the standard deviation of one roll of a fair die.

blocks.title: Same mean, different risk
blocks.q: Game A pays \$45 or \$55, each with probability $\frac12$. Game B pays \$20 or \$80, each with probability $\frac12$. Compare.
steps: A: every payout is 5 from the mean, so $\sigma_A = 5$. B: every payout is 30 from the mean, so $\sigma_B = 30$.
B is much riskier: its outcomes land far from the mean.

blocks.name: dice
blocks.cap: One die: values spread from 1 to 6 around the mean 3.5, a typical distance of about 1.7.

blocks.html: Forgetting to weight by probability (just averaging the squared distances as if every value were equally likely), or forgetting the final square root. Check: σ should look like a typical distance from the mean, in the same units as X.
